On the admissible record, rejection is defensible only as a conservative procurement decision made before approval readiness was established: BPROC-008-D shows an unresolved storage-control inconsistency with no logged failed test, BPROC-008-C shows the quality process was informal and not documented in a reviewed binder, BPROC-008-B shows mixed but not clean delivery history because one quality artifact was late, and BPROC-008-E shows the file itself contemplated follow-up before approval if storage controls remained unresolved. Read together, those items support that the vendor never cleared diligence cleanly and that proceeding was not required. They do not support a stronger claim that a reject-level control failure was proved.
output.claims_about_business_cost: Reopening the vendor review would delay staffing and create avoidable churn without obviously improving the admissible record. Residual uncertainty can be handled by recording the rationale as non-approval under unresolved diligence risk rather than escalating to reconstruct a stronger rejection theory that the current admissible file does not support.
output.claims_about_policy: Policy text cuts both ways. It bars characterizing questionnaire inconsistencies and quality-process gaps as proof of a reject-level control failure, so the packet should not make that claim. But the same policy allows rejection where admissible due-diligence evidence shows a material unresolved risk. The compliant framing is therefore: rejection was based on unresolved diligence risk at decision time, not on a confirmed failure. Because BPROC-008-D remained unresolved in the file and BPROC-008-E ties unresolved storage controls to pre-approval follow-up, the admissible record can support caveated compliance if the auditor accepts that approval readiness was not established rather than demanding proof of a formal control breach.
